screens.title: Control Flow: Conditionals and Loops
screens.subtitle: Make decisions and repeat actions to power interactive gameplay

narration.text: Control flow is what transforms static code into interactive behavior. In Unity, conditionals allow your scripts to take different paths when conditions change, and loops let you repeat tasks without copying code. Together they let a game react to player input, manage enemy waves, and enforce game rules. In this chapter you will learn the mechanics of if, else if, else, switch with enums, and the loop family: for, while, do-while, and foreach. You will see concrete examples: a health-check that changes UI and state, a switch on game state using an enumeration, a for loop that spawns enemies, and a foreach loop that iterates an inventory list. We will also surface common mistakes — missing braces, off-by-one errors, and infinite loops — and practical best practices like caching references and avoiding heavy work inside Update. By the end you will be able to choose the right control flow structure for gameplay logic and reason about performance implications. Consider how a single condition or a small loop can change the entire feel of a scene; that is the power we’ll unlock together.

keyIdea.title: Why control flow matters
keyIdea.text: Conditionals and loops let your game react and iterate. They form the decision-making backbone of gameplay and must be used with care for correctness and performance.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Control Flow Overview
Control Flow: Conditionals and Loops
Decide what runs and when. Build reactive and repeatable gameplay logic.

Control flow determines the path and repetition of execution. In Unity this means responding to input, managing states, and iterating collections. We'll map each construct to common gameplay tasks so you can select the right tool when designing systems like health, spawning, and inventory.

In this lesson
How to use if, switch, and loops to implement gameplay decisions and repetitions.
Interactive Concept Map
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Conditionals
If/else chains and switch with enums decide game responses like health warnings or game state changes.
Loops
For, foreach, while repeat work: spawning enemies, iterating inventory, or retrying actions.
// Example: health check if (currentHealth <= 0) { GameOver(); } else if (currentHealth < 30) { WarnLowHealth(); }
Conditionals
Choose execution paths based on true or false checks.
Switch & Enums
Map discrete states like menus and pause to clean handling.
Loops & Performance
Repeat safely and avoid heavy work per frame.
Explore these topics to build reliable and efficient gameplay logic.

narration.text: Across the next screens you'll develop concrete skills for reliable gameplay logic. First, you'll learn to implement conditional statements like if, else if, else, and switch so your code can pick different behaviors at runtime. We'll show how this maps to common game actions: health checks, state transitions, and UI changes. Second, you'll use looping constructs: for when you know the number of iterations, foreach to traverse collections safely, and while or do-while when a repeat-until condition is needed. Third, you will apply control flow to gameplay: toggle running, spawn enemies with a for loop, and iterate inventory with foreach. Finally, you'll surface common pitfalls and performance best practices such as avoiding expensive operations every frame, caching references, and preventing infinite loops. For each objective you'll see a visual mnemonic and a competency milestone so you can confirm mastery. These skills matter because they turn isolated code into predictable, maintainable systems that scale from prototypes to complete scenes.

screens.title: What is Control Flow?
screens.subtitle: The execution order and decision logic that make programs interactive

narration.text: Control flow is the rulebook a program follows to decide which statements run and when. In practical terms, it answers two questions: should this block run now, and should we do it again? Conditionals answer the first question by evaluating boolean expressions and choosing paths, while loops answer the second by repeating a block as long as a condition holds. In games this is vital: input must produce immediate responses, AI must update behavior each frame or at intervals, and spawning systems iterate sets of objects. A common misconception is that control flow is only about branching; in fact the choice of when and where you check conditions matters just as much. For example, checking health inside an event fired on damage is usually more efficient and semantically correct than polling health each frame. Concrete example: checking if playerHealth is below a threshold triggers UI feedback and sound effects. Contrast this with a poll inside Update which runs constantly even when no change occurred. Takeaway: design where conditions are evaluated intentionally, choose event-driven checks when possible, and use loops where repetition is explicit and bounded. How might you change design if polling causes visible frame drops?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Control flow governs branch decisions and repetition; design checks and loops to reflect gameplay intent and performance constraints.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is Control Flow?
Execution order, decisions, and repetition that produce interactive behavior.
Key points
  • Branching chooses alternate code paths based on boolean conditions.
  • Loops repeat a block while a condition remains true or for a defined count.
  • Where you evaluate conditions affects correctness and performance.
Analogy
Think of conditionals as forks on a trail and loops as a treadmill that repeats steps until you stop it.
Key Takeaway

Control flow should reflect game intent: use events when possible, loops when repetition is bounded, and keep checks minimal per frame.

Example: Damage-triggered health check
// In a damage event handler
public void ApplyDamage(int damage) {
    currentHealth -= damage;
    if (currentHealth <= 0) {
        TriggerGameOver();
    } else if (currentHealth < 30) {
        PlayLowHealthWarning();
    }
}
This example fires only when damage occurs, avoiding per-frame checks and making intent clear. It reduces unnecessary work and eliminates timing-related bugs.
Common Mistake
Polling health each frame in Update when damage events exist leads to wasted cycles.
Check Yourself
If a check runs every frame, ask if it can be event-driven or rate-limited.

narration.text: If statements evaluate a boolean condition to decide whether to run a block of code. An else if provides an additional test when the first condition is false, and else is a final fallback when none of the earlier tests apply. Use them when you need mutually exclusive outcomes. For example, a health check that logs defeat, warns on low health, or reports normal state maps naturally to an if, else if, else chain. A common mistake is omitting braces for single-line blocks and later adding lines that execute outside the intended branch. Another subtle issue is using multiple independent ifs when you mean an exclusive chain; independent ifs will evaluate every test and may produce conflicting actions. Concrete example: if you check currentHealth <= 0 and then separately check currentHealth < 30 with two independent ifs, both could run when health is zero, causing duplicated behavior. Best practices: prefer clear else if chains for exclusive conditions, keep conditions simple and readable, and add logging during development to verify the active path. Consider whether a switch or enum better expresses multiple discrete states, especially when branching on a single variable.

keyIdea.title: Branching
keyIdea.text: Use if / else if / else for mutually exclusive checks; avoid independent ifs when exclusivity is intended.

content.html:
Definition
If, Else If, Else
Create exclusive paths based on boolean expressions.
Process: Typical if-chain
  1. Evaluate the first boolean condition.
  2. If true, execute its block and skip the rest.
  3. If false, evaluate the next else if condition, if present.
  4. If none match, run the else fallback if provided.
Pro Tip
Keep each condition focused on a single concept, avoid complex combined logic inside one condition.
Common Mistake
Omitting braces or using separate ifs when exclusivity is required causes logic errors.
Example: Health evaluation
// Evaluate player health
if (currentHealth <= 0) {
    Debug.Log("Player is defeated!");
} else if (currentHealth < 30) {
    Debug.Log("Warning: Low health!");
} else if (currentHealth < 70) {
    Debug.Log("Player is moderately injured.");
} else {
    Debug.Log("Player health is good.");
}
This chain ensures exactly one message runs per evaluation. It avoids multiple conflicting actions and communicates intent clearly.
Key Takeaway

Use else if chains for mutually exclusive checks and add braces even for single-line blocks to prevent later errors.

screens.title: Switch and Enums
screens.subtitle: Cleanly dispatch behavior based on discrete state values

narration.text: The switch statement lets you evaluate a single expression and dispatch execution to different cases. When paired with an enum, it becomes a clear, readable mapping from named states to behaviors. For example, an enum representing GameState — StartMenu, Playing, Paused, GameOver — can be handled in a switch to enable or disable UI, player input, or enemy AI. Compared to long else-if chains, a switch emphasizes that only one variable determines the outcome. A common misconception is that switch is limited; modern usage handles enums and can include a default fallback to catch unexpected values. Always remember to include a break to avoid fall-through unless fall-through is intentional. Concrete example: handling pause toggles reliably disables input and pauses time. If you attempted this with multiple independent if statements, you might enable and disable systems in conflicting orders. Best practice: prefer enums for small sets of named states, and keep each case focused and minimal to preserve readability and testability. Switch and Enums means use switch with enums for single-variable multiple-choice logic; it improves readability and ensures exclusive handling of discrete states.. In practical terms, cleanly dispatch behavior based on discrete state values. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Switch vs else-if
keyIdea.text: Use switch with enums for single-variable multiple-choice logic; it improves readability and ensures exclusive handling of discrete states.

content.html:
Definition
Switch & Enums
Map named discrete values to specific behavior branches.
When to choose switch
  • When decisions depend on a single variable with multiple known values.
  • When you want readable, maintainable mappings between states and actions.
  • When you want a default fallback for unexpected values.
Example: GameState handling
public enum GameState { StartMenu, Playing, Paused, GameOver }

void HandleGameState(GameState state) {
    switch (state) {
        case GameState.StartMenu:
            ShowStartMenu();
            break;
        case GameState.Playing:
            EnableGameplay();
            break;
        case GameState.Paused:
            PauseGame();
            break;
        case GameState.GameOver:
            ShowGameOver();
            break;
        default:
            Debug.LogWarning("Unknown game state!");
            break;
    }
}
Each case executes exclusively. The default branch protects against unexpected enum values, which is especially useful during refactors.
Pro Tip
Use enums to document allowed states and make switch exhaustive when possible.
Common Mistake
Forgetting break can cause unintentional fall-through. Use comments if fall-through is intentional.

screens.title: Health System: If-chain in Update (Example)
screens.subtitle: Walk through a real Unity C# health-check pattern

narration.text: Let's walk a concrete health-check example that appears often in Unity projects. In a simple HealthSystem script you might update the player's currentHealth in response to damage events, but you could also demonstrate checks in Update for teaching. The important point is how the if, else if, else chain maps health values to messages or state changes. In practice, prefer event-driven checks when damage triggers a handler, but understanding this pattern is critical. In this example the chain checks for defeat first, then low health, then moderate injury, and finally healthy. A concrete pitfall is testing thresholds in the wrong order. If you check currentHealth < 70 before checking < 30, the low health block may never run. Another mistake is using assignment instead of comparison inside conditions, which is a syntax error in C# but common for beginners from other languages. For debugging, add clear logs and test edge values: zero, exact threshold, and just above threshold to confirm the branches. Your takeaway: order your conditions from most specific to most general and prefer event triggers over per-frame polls when possible.

keyIdea.title: Code walkthrough
keyIdea.text: Order conditions from most specific to most general; test edge cases and prefer event-driven checks for state changes.

content.html:
Process Flow
Health System Example
Understand ordering, edge cases, and event-driven alternatives.
Checks to verify
  • Threshold ordering from smallest to largest where appropriate.
  • Handling exact boundaries like zero or threshold values.
  • Use events rather than Update polling when damage is discrete.
Check Yourself
Try damage values that land exactly on thresholds and confirm only one branch runs.
Code (illustrative)
using UnityEngine;

public class HealthSystem : MonoBehaviour {
    public int currentHealth = 100;

    void Update() {
        if (currentHealth <= 0) {
            Debug.Log("Player is defeated! Game Over.");
        } else if (currentHealth < 30) {
            Debug.Log("Warning: Low health!");
        } else if (currentHealth < 70) {
            Debug.Log("Player is moderately injured.");
        } else {
            Debug.Log("Player health is good.");
        }

        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space)) {
            TakeDamage(10);
        }
    }

    public void TakeDamage(int damageAmount) {
        currentHealth -= damageAmount;
        Debug.Log("Took " + damageAmount + " damage. Current Health: " + currentHealth);
    }
}
Use the code as a lab starting point, but in real projects prefer event-based damage handlers to avoid per-frame polling of state.

screens.title: Loops Overview
screens.subtitle: When and how to repeat work safely

narration.text: Loops let you repeat a block of code without copying it. Common loop types in C# are for, foreach, while, and do-while. Use for when you know or can bound the number of iterations, such as spawning a fixed number of enemies. Use foreach to iterate collections like arrays or lists when the index is not needed, which reduces off-by-one errors. Use while when you need to loop until a condition changes in complex ways, but be careful: if the condition is not guaranteed to change, you can create an infinite loop that freezes Unity. Do-while guarantees the block runs at least once before the condition is checked, which can be useful for retry attempts or prompting logic. A typical misconception is to use while for everything; prefer for or foreach for indexable collections and when iteration count is known. Practical tip: validate collection references before looping to avoid null reference exceptions. Example: iterating inventory items with foreach prints each item name and avoids index arithmetic. Always think about exit conditions and whether a loop belongs in Update or in a single method invoked by an event.

keyIdea.title: Loop types
keyIdea.text: Choose for for bounded iterations, foreach for collection traversal, while/do-while for condition-driven repetition; always ensure a safe exit.

content.html:
Core Concept
Loops Overview
Repeat tasks with control over iteration and exit conditions.
for
Best for known counts like spawning N enemies; manage indexes carefully to avoid off-by-one errors.
foreach
Iterate collections without manual index handling; safer and more readable when index is not needed.
while
Run until a condition becomes false; ensure the condition will change to avoid infinite loops.
do-while
Guarantees at least one execution; useful for retry loops or prompts that must run once.
Key Takeaway

Match the loop type to the task: use bounded loops for counts and foreach for safe traversal; always validate exit conditions.

Example: Inventory with foreach
public string[] itemNames = { "Sword", "Shield", "Potion" };

void DisplayInventory() {
    foreach (string item in itemNames) {
        Debug.Log("Inventory item: " + item);
    }
}
This example is concise and avoids index math, which reduces off-by-one risks. Foreach is ideal when you only need the element, not its position.
Warning
Using while without a guaranteed exit or validation can create infinite loops and freeze the Editor.

screens.title: For Loop: Spawning Enemies
screens.subtitle: A bounded iteration example for instantiation and logging

narration.text: The for loop is ideal when the number of iterations is known ahead of time. In the EnemySpawner example we specify how many enemies to spawn and loop from zero up to that count. Each iteration calculates a random position within a radius, keeps the Y coordinate consistent, instantiates a prefab, and logs the action. Key safety checks are included: validate the prefab reference before entering the loop to avoid null instantiation and early return if the prefab is missing. A common off-by-one mistake is using i <= numberOfEnemiesToSpawn which spawns one too many; prefer i < numberOfEnemiesToSpawn for zero-based counts. For performance, do instantiation in Start or when a spawn event occurs rather than in Update, unless you intentionally spawn over time. For large numbers consider object pooling rather than repeated Instantiate and Destroy calls. Concrete example: spawning five simple cube enemies in Start mimics wave creation; trying to spawn thousands without pooling will spike memory and frame time. Takeaway: for loops are simple and efficient for bounded work, but validate references, watch index bounds, and consider pooling for heavy or repeated instantiation.

keyIdea.title: For loops
keyIdea.text: Use for loops for a fixed number of iterations; check bounds, validate references, and prefer pooling for high-volume instantiation.

content.html:
Process
Spawning with for
Instantiate a known number of enemies safely and predictably.
Spawner checklist
  • Validate enemyPrefab is assigned before looping.
  • Use i < count for zero-based arrays to avoid off-by-one.
  • Keep expensive calculations outside the loop if possible.
Analogy
Think of a for loop as a conveyor belt that runs a fixed number of items through the same steps.
Example: EnemySpawner
public GameObject enemyPrefab;
public int numberOfEnemiesToSpawn = 5;
public float spawnRadius = 10f;

void Start() {
    if (enemyPrefab == null) {
        Debug.LogError("Enemy Prefab is not assigned to EnemySpawner!");
        return;
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < numberOfEnemiesToSpawn; i++) {
        Vector3 randomPos = transform.position + Random.insideUnitSphere * spawnRadius;
        randomPos.y = transform.position.y;
        Instantiate(enemyPrefab, randomPos, Quaternion.identity);
        Debug.Log("Spawned enemy #" + (i + 1) + " at " + randomPos);
    }
}
This pattern is clear and bounded. Replace Instantiate with pool retrieval for heavy spawn scenarios to avoid allocation spikes.

screens.title: Foreach vs For
screens.subtitle: Readable collection traversal versus index control

narration.text: When iterating collections in C#, you have a choice: use for when you need the index or must modify elements by position, and use foreach when you simply need each element. Foreach improves readability and reduces off-by-one mistakes because it abstracts the index away. For example, printing each inventory item is concise with foreach and less error-prone than using a for loop with manual bounds. However, foreach does not allow modifying the collection structure during iteration, and in certain performance-sensitive contexts a for loop can be marginally faster for indexed lists. A common misunderstanding is that foreach is always slower; in typical game code for modest collections the convenience and readability outweigh tiny performance differences. If you must remove items while iterating, consider iterating backward with a for loop or collecting removals and applying them afterward. Concrete example: using foreach to log item names is clear and self-documenting. Takeaway: prefer foreach for simple traversal and readability; use for when you need index access, removal during iteration, or micro-optimizations backed by profiling. Foreach vs For means choose foreach for readability and safety, for when you need indexes or must modify or remove elements during iteration.. In practical terms, readable collection traversal versus index control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Traversal choice
keyIdea.text: Choose foreach for readability and safety, for when you need indexes or must modify or remove elements during iteration.

content.html:
Comparison
Foreach vs For
Readability versus index control and modification power.
foreach example
foreach (string item in itemNames) {
    Debug.Log("Inventory item: " + item);
}
for example (when index needed)
for (int i = 0; i < items.Count; i++) {
    Debug.Log("Item " + i + ": " + items[i]);
}
When to prefer each
  • Foreach: simple read-only traversal, reduced off-by-one risk.
  • For: need index, remove items safely by iterating backward, or micro-opt when profiling shows benefit.
  • Never modify the collection structure inside a foreach; use a safe pattern instead.
Pro Tip
If you must remove items, iterate from the end toward zero using a for loop to preserve correctness.

narration.text: While and do-while loops repeat code based on a condition. A while loop checks the condition before each iteration, making it suitable when the repeat might be skipped entirely. A do-while loop runs the body first and checks the condition afterwards, guaranteeing at least one execution. These loops are useful for retry logic, waiting for a resource, or performing an operation until a success condition occurs. The major risk is an infinite loop: if the loop condition never becomes false, the program will hang and Unity can freeze. A common mistake is forgetting to update the loop variable or relying on external state that will not change. Concrete example: waiting for a simulated network retry may use do-while to attempt once and repeat until success, but you should include a maximum retry count to prevent endless repetition. Best practice: always include a deterministic exit condition or a safe counter, and avoid running long loops on the main thread during a frame. Consider moving blocking retry logic to a coroutine or asynchronous task to keep the frame responsive. While and Do-While Loops means always guarantee a loop will terminate by tying the condition to predictable state changes or adding a maximum iteration limit.. In practical terms, condition-driven repetition and its risks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Exit safety
keyIdea.text: Always guarantee a loop will terminate by tying the condition to predictable state changes or adding a maximum iteration limit.

content.html:
Definition
While & Do-While
Use for condition-driven repetition; always ensure termination.
Safety checklist
  • Ensure the condition can change and become false.
  • Add max iteration counters for retries to avoid infinite loops.
  • Offload long waits to coroutines or async tasks to avoid blocking frames.
Example: Safe retry
int attempts = 0;
const int maxAttempts = 5;
bool success = false;

while (!success && attempts < maxAttempts) {
    success = TryAction();
    attempts++;
}

if (!success) Debug.Log("Action failed after retries");
This pattern prevents infinite loops by bounding attempts. In Unity, consider using a coroutine with yields between retries to avoid blocking the main thread.
Warning
Never run potentially long while loops directly inside Update; they can freeze the Editor.

screens.title: Performance and Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Where to run checks and how to avoid costly per-frame work

narration.text: Performance is a practical constraint when using control flow. Heavy calculations or repeated searches inside Update or tight loops can reduce frame rates. A frequent issue is calling GameObject. Find or expensive queries inside loops per frame; instead, cache references in Start or Awake. For loops that iterate many elements each frame, consider whether the work can be spread over multiple frames, precomputed, or optimized with spatial partitioning. Foreach is readable, but for very large collections profiling may reveal a small overhead compared to an indexed for loop; only optimize after measuring. Another best practice is to move logic that only needs to run on events into event handlers rather than Update. For example, health checks run when damage occurs, spawning can run in Start or via coroutines for staggered spawn, and UI updates can be driven by state change events. Concrete example: replacing a per-frame search in Update with a cached reference in Start removed dozens of microseconds per frame in many projects. Takeaway: design control flow with profiling and correctness in mind, cache what you can, avoid allocations in hot paths, and use pooling for frequent instantiation.

keyIdea.title: Performance rules
keyIdea.text: Avoid heavy per-frame work, cache references, profile before micro-optimizing, and use pooling for frequent instantiation.

content.html:
Process Flow
Performance & Best Practices
Design where and how checks run to protect frame rate and correctness.
Checklist for hot paths
  • Cache references in Start/Awake, avoid GameObject.Find in Update or loops.
  • Move event-driven checks out of Update when possible.
  • Use object pooling for frequent Instantiate/Destroy patterns.
Pro Tip
Profile before optimizing. Small code changes can have large effects only when in a hot path.
Example: Cache instead of find
GameObject player;

void Start() {
    player = GameObject.FindWithTag("Player"); // do this once
}

void Update() {
    if (player == null) return;
    // use cached player reference here, not find each frame
}
This small change avoids repeated scene searches. For spawn-heavy systems, use a pooling pattern to reuse objects and prevent frequent allocations.
Key Takeaway

Design control flow with intent: choose event-driven checks, cache what you can, and profile hot loops to guide optimization.

narration.text: Let's recap the essential concepts to remember. First, control flow determines which statements run and how often: conditionals pick execution paths, and loops repeat actions. Second, choose the right conditional: if chains for simple exclusive checks, switch with enums for discrete state dispatch, and always include a default to catch unexpected values. Third, select the proper loop type: for for bounded counts, foreach for safe collection traversal, while/do-while for condition-driven repetition, and always guarantee loop termination. Finally, avoid per-frame expensive operations, cache references, and prefer object pooling for frequent instantiation. These rules help your gameplay systems stay correct and performant. Keep these concepts in mind when you design health systems, spawners, or inventory loops and test edge cases and boundaries during playtesting. Key Concepts means branch clearly, iterate safely, and optimize only after profiling; guard against infinite loops and off-by-one errors.. In practical terms, what to remember. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Concise summary
keyIdea.text: Branch clearly, iterate safely, and optimize only after profiling; guard against infinite loops and off-by-one errors.

If, else if, else, and switch let you choose code paths based on conditions or state.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three practical reminders before you code

narration.text: Before you start coding, keep three practical reminders in mind. First, prefer event-driven checks for discrete changes and reserve per-frame checks for continuous conditions that truly need them. Second, validate loop bounds and collection references; off-by-one and null references are common sources of runtime errors. Third, profile and optimize only after identifying hot paths; simple caching and pooling often yield large benefits. These reminders will save debugging time and keep your gameplay responsive during playtests. As you implement the hands-on activity, use them as quick checks before hitting Play in the Editor. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means event-driven checks, validated loops, and targeted profiling keep gameplay systems reliable and performant.. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical reminders
keyIdea.text: Event-driven checks, validated loops, and targeted profiling keep gameplay systems reliable and performant.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Quick Reference
Event-driven checks
Run logic on events like damage or state change instead of polling when possible.
Validate loops
